questions.q: Which of these is a homogeneous mixture?
o: Soda water (carbon dioxide dissolved in water)
questions.a: Soda water: carbon dioxide dissolved in water has the same composition throughout, so it is a homogeneous mixture (a solution).

questions.q: A shiny bar looks like a single metal. Its maker says it was made by melting about 80 parts of copper with 20 parts of tin and letting the melt cool. Which description of the bar is correct?
o: It is bronze, a homogeneous mixture whose metals cannot be separated by physical methods
It is brass, a heterogeneous mixture of copper and tin
It is a pure substance, because it looks like a single metal
It is bronze, a heterogeneous mixture because it contains two metals
questions.a: It is bronze, a homogeneous mixture whose metals cannot be separated by physical methods: an alloy of about 80% copper and 20% tin is bronze, and an alloy is a homogeneous mixture.

questions.q: Match each mixture in Column I with what it is made of in Column II. Column I: 1. Smoke; 2. Fog; 3. Brass; 4. Rocket fuel mixture. Column II: (a) tiny liquid water droplets in air; (b) hydrogen and oxygen gases; (c) solid particles suspended in air; (d) about 80% copper and 20% zinc.
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b: smoke is solid particles in air, fog is tiny water droplets in air, brass is about 80% copper and 20% zinc, and the rocket fuel mixture is hydrogen and oxygen.

questions.q: True or False: 'In a well-stirred glass of sugar water, the last sip is sweeter than the first sip.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Sugar water is a homogeneous mixture (a solution) with a uniform composition throughout, so the first and the last sip are equally sweet.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: a solution has a uniform composition, so every sip is equally sweet

questions.q: (a) What is a heterogeneous mixture? (b) Give one example of a heterogeneous mixture from your kitchen.
questions.a: (a) A heterogeneous mixture is one whose composition is not uniform; its components can be seen separately, as sand particles can be seen in sand and water. (b) Oil and water (or sand and water).
s: (a) A mixture with non-uniform composition whose components are visibly distinct
(b) A correct example, such as oil and water

questions.q: Air, smoke and fog all have a gas as one component. (a) Is air (a mixture of gases) homogeneous or heterogeneous? (b) What is suspended in the air in smoke, and is smoke homogeneous or heterogeneous? (c) What is present in the air in fog, and is fog homogeneous or heterogeneous?
questions.a: (a) Homogeneous: gas particles move freely in all directions and mix uniformly, so most mixtures of gases are homogeneous. (b) Solid particles are suspended in air; smoke is heterogeneous. (c) Tiny liquid water droplets are present in air; fog is heterogeneous.
s: (a) Air is homogeneous, as gases mix uniformly
(b) Smoke: solid particles in air, heterogeneous
(c) Fog: tiny water droplets in air, heterogeneous

questions.q: Meena stirs yellow sulfur powder with grey iron filings. Under a hand lens she can still see separate yellow and grey bits. Which conclusion is correct?
o: It is a heterogeneous mixture, and a magnet can pull the iron filings out of it
It is a homogeneous mixture, because both components are fine powders
It is a heterogeneous mixture, but it cannot be separated because both components are solids
It is a homogeneous mixture, so its components cannot be separated by a physical method
questions.a: It is a heterogeneous mixture, and a magnet can pull the iron filings out of it: the yellow and grey bits stay visibly distinct, so the mixture is not uniform, and a property of one solid (iron is attracted by a magnet) can be used to separate the mixture, as iron nails are separated from sawdust.

questions.q: Four students classify mixtures as homogeneous (Hm) or heterogeneous (Ht). Asha: air Hm, smoke Hm. Bilal: brass Ht, fog Ht. Chitra: vinegar Hm, muddy water Ht, brass Hm. Dev: soda water Hm, fog Hm. (i) Which student is correct in every entry? (ii) Correct Asha's error and give the reason. (iii) Correct Bilal's error and give the reason.
questions.a: (i) Chitra: vinegar is a solution (Hm), muddy water has visible particles that settle (Ht) and brass is an alloy (Hm). (ii) Smoke is Ht, not Hm: it is solid particles suspended in air. (iii) Brass is Hm, not Ht: it is an alloy, a homogeneous mixture of copper and zinc formed by melting and mixing.
s: (i) Chitra is fully correct
(ii) Smoke is heterogeneous: solid particles suspended in air
(iii) Brass is homogeneous: it is an alloy

questions.q: Kiran stirs one spoon of common salt and one spoon of sand into 100 mL of water in a beaker and leaves it to stand. (a) Describe what she will see in the beaker after ten minutes. (b) Classify the whole mixture in the beaker and give the reason. (c) She then filters the mixture. What is left on the filter paper, and is the filtrate homogeneous or heterogeneous? (d) Kiran concludes, 'Filtering turned a heterogeneous mixture into a homogeneous one, so filtering changes the type of a mixture.' Judge her conclusion.
questions.a: (a) The salt dissolves and cannot be seen, while the sand particles stay visible and settle at the bottom. (b) Heterogeneous: the composition is not uniform, because the sand is visibly distinct and settles with time. (c) The sand is left on the filter paper as a residue; the filtrate is salt water, a homogeneous mixture (a solution). (d) She is wrong: filtering only removed the sand. The salt water was a homogeneous solution all along (a solution always remains homogeneous); what she has now is a different mixture with one component fewer, not the same mixture changed in type.
s: (a) Salt dissolves; sand stays visible and settles
(b) Heterogeneous: non-uniform, sand visible and settles
(c) Sand on the filter paper; filtrate is a homogeneous salt solution
(d) Conclusion wrong: filtering removed the sand; the salt solution was homogeneous all along

questions.q: Assertion (A): Bronze cannot be separated into copper and tin by a physical method such as filtering. Reason (R): Bronze is a heterogeneous mixture whose particles are too small to be seen.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: physical methods cannot separate an alloy, but bronze is a homogeneous mixture of copper and tin, not a heterogeneous one.

questions.q: Ravi dissolves 15 g of sugar in 135 g of water. What is the mass by mass percentage of sugar in the solution?
questions.a: 10% m/m: mass of solution = 15 g + 135 g = 150 g, and (15/150) x 100 = 10%.

questions.q: A bottle of glucose solution is labelled 5% m/v. What does this label mean?
o: 5 g of glucose is present in every 100 mL of the solution
5 g of glucose is dissolved in 100 mL of water
5 g of glucose is present in every 100 g of the solution
5 mL of glucose is present in every 100 mL of the solution
questions.a: 5 g of glucose is present in every 100 mL of the solution: mass by volume percentage gives the grams of solute in 100 millilitres of the solution.

questions.q: A school lab has 300 mL of alcohol. How much water must be mixed with all of it to make a hand sanitiser that is 60% v/v alcohol? (Take the volumes to add up.)
questions.a: 200 mL: at 60% v/v, the 300 mL of alcohol must be 60% of the solution, so the solution is 300/0.60 = 500 mL, and the water needed is 500 - 300 = 200 mL.

questions.q: Read the statements. I. Dissolving 20 g of salt in 80 g of water gives a 20% m/m solution. II. Dissolving 20 g of salt in water to make 80 mL of solution gives a 20% m/v solution. III. For the same solution, the % m/m and the % w/w values are numerically equal. Which of these are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. I: 20/(20 + 80) x 100 = 20% m/m. II is wrong: 20/80 x 100 = 25% m/v, not 20%. III: weight and mass are used interchangeably, so % m/m and % w/w are equal.

questions.q: (a) What is meant by the concentration of a solution? (b) Why can we not add any amount of salt and sugar to a fixed amount of water and still call it ORS?
questions.a: (a) Concentration is the amount of solute dissolved in a given amount of solvent or solution. (b) ORS needs specified amounts of salt and sugar in a fixed amount of water; changing these amounts gives a salt and sugar solution that is not ORS, because the right proportion is essential.
s: (a) Amount of solute in a given amount of solvent or solution
(b) ORS needs fixed amounts in the right proportion; other amounts are not ORS

questions.q: True or False: 'Mass by mass percentage is used only for homogeneous mixtures.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Mass by mass percentage is also used for heterogeneous mixtures such as milk powder and spice mixtures, and to label how much salt, sugar or protein packaged foods contain.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: it is also used for heterogeneous mixtures such as milk powder and spice mixtures

questions.q: Neha dissolves 30 g of sugar in 120 g of water. (a) Find the mass of the solution. (b) Find its mass by mass percentage. (c) Keeping the same 120 g of water, how much more sugar must she dissolve to make the solution 25% m/m?
questions.a: (a) 30 g + 120 g = 150 g. (b) (30/150) x 100 = 20% m/m. (c) For 25% m/m the sugar must be 25% of the solution: with x g of sugar, x/(x + 120) = 0.25, so x = 40 g. She must add 40 - 30 = 10 g more sugar.
s: (a) Mass of solution = 150 g
(c) 40 g sugar needed, so 10 g more

questions.q: Solution P has 10 g of glucose in 200 mL of solution. Solution Q has 12 g of glucose in 300 mL of solution. (i) Find the % m/v of P. (ii) Find the % m/v of Q. (iii) Q contains more glucose. Explain whether it is the more concentrated solution.
questions.a: (i) P: (10/200) x 100 = 5% m/v. (ii) Q: (12/300) x 100 = 4% m/v. (iii) No. Concentration compares the solute with the amount of solution; Q has more glucose but it is spread through a larger volume, so P (5%) is more concentrated than Q (4%).
s: (i) P = 5% m/v
(ii) Q = 4% m/v
(iii) P is more concentrated; concentration depends on solute per volume of solution

questions.q: Answer each part in one step. (a) 8 g of salt is dissolved in 92 g of water. Find the % m/m. (b) 3 g of glucose is dissolved in water to make 60 mL of solution. Find the % m/v. (c) 30 mL of alcohol is mixed with water to make 200 mL of solution. Find the % v/v. (d) How much salt is present in 400 mL of 0.9% m/v saline? (e) How much acetic acid is present in 300 mL of vinegar that is 5% v/v acetic acid?
s: (d) 3.6 g of salt
(e) 15 mL of acetic acid

questions.q: A pickle maker in Guntur prepares salt brine in two batches. Batch 1: 120 g of salt dissolved in 880 g of water. Batch 2: 90 g of salt dissolved in 510 g of water. Her recipe says the brine must be 12% m/m; a stronger brine makes the pickle too salty. (a) Find the % m/m of batch 1. (b) Find the % m/m of batch 2. (c) Which batch follows the recipe, and which is saltier? (d) How much water must she add to batch 2 to bring it to 12% m/m?
questions.a: (a) 120/(120 + 880) x 100 = 120/1000 x 100 = 12% m/m. (b) 90/(90 + 510) x 100 = 90/600 x 100 = 15% m/m. (c) Batch 1 follows the recipe; batch 2 (15%) is saltier. (d) For 12%, 90 g of salt must be 12% of the solution: 90/0.12 = 750 g of solution. It now weighs 600 g, so she must add 750 - 600 = 150 g of water.
s: (a) Batch 1 = 12% m/m
(b) Batch 2 = 15% m/m
(c) Batch 1 follows the recipe; batch 2 is saltier
(d) 750 g solution needed, so add 150 g water

questions.q: What is a saturated solution?
o: A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature
A solution in which the solute and solvent have equal masses
A solution that has been heated until it boils
A solution in which no solute has dissolved yet
questions.a: A saturated solution is one that cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature.

questions.q: How does the solubility of a gas dissolved in a liquid generally change when the temperature of the liquid rises?
o: It first increases and then becomes zero
questions.a: It generally decreases: unlike solid solutes, gases dissolved in liquids become less soluble as the temperature rises.

questions.q: Using Table 5.4 (ammonium chloride: 55 g per 100 g of water at 60 degrees Celsius and 37 g per 100 g of water at 20 degrees Celsius), a saturated solution of ammonium chloride made with 200 g of water at 60 degrees Celsius is cooled to 20 degrees Celsius. What mass of ammonium chloride separates out?
questions.a: 36 g: 200 g of water holds 2 x 55 = 110 g at 60 degrees Celsius but only 2 x 37 = 74 g at 20 degrees Celsius, so 110 - 74 = 36 g separates out.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Cooling a hot saturated solution of sodium chloride from 80 degrees Celsius to 10 degrees Celsius gives very little sodium chloride as crystals. Reason (R): According to Table 5.4, the solubility of sodium chloride changes only from 37 g to 36 g per 100 g of water over this range.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: crystals form from the solute that no longer stays dissolved, and since the solubility of sodium chloride falls by only about 1 g per 100 g of water, very little separates on cooling.

questions.q: (a) What is a crystal? (b) Name two crystals you can see in everyday life.
questions.a: (a) A crystal is a solid made up of particles arranged in a regular geometric pattern. (b) Any two of: rock salt, sugar crystals of candy sugar (mishri), snowflakes, frost on windows.
s: (a) A solid with particles in a regular geometric pattern
(b) Two correct examples, such as rock salt and snowflakes

questions.q: Using Table 5.4 (potassium nitrate: 106 g per 100 g of water at 60 degrees Celsius and 32 g at 20 degrees Celsius), a student saturates some water with potassium nitrate at 60 degrees Celsius and finds that 53 g has dissolved. (a) What mass of water did she use? (b) What mass of potassium nitrate separates out when the solution is cooled to 20 degrees Celsius?
questions.a: (a) 106 g dissolves in 100 g of water, so 53 g needs 53/106 x 100 = 50 g of water. (b) At 20 degrees Celsius, 50 g of water holds 32/2 = 16 g, so 53 - 16 = 37 g separates out.
s: (a) 50 g of water
(b) 53 - 16 = 37 g separates out

questions.q: In Activity 5.3, copper sulfate crystals are prepared. (a) Why is the hot saturated solution filtered? (b) Why is the filtrate allowed to cool slowly without disturbing it? (c) What is the use of the drop of dilute sulfuric acid?
questions.a: (a) To remove insoluble impurities. (b) Slow cooling gives the particles enough time to come together, forming larger, shiny, well-shaped crystals. (c) It helps in making pure crystals by preventing unwanted reactions.
s: (a) To remove insoluble impurities
(b) Slow cooling gives larger, well-shaped crystals
(c) Sulfuric acid prevents unwanted reactions, giving pure crystals

questions.q: From the solubility curve in Fig. 5.6, compound 'B' has a solubility of 287 g per 100 g of water at 60 degrees Celsius and 241 g per 100 g of water at 40 degrees Celsius. A saturated solution of B is made with 250 g of water at 60 degrees Celsius and cooled to 40 degrees Celsius. (i) What mass of B separates for every 100 g of water? (ii) What total mass of B separates? (iii) Is the liquid left at 40 degrees Celsius saturated or not? Give a reason.
questions.a: (i) 287 - 241 = 46 g per 100 g of water. (ii) 250 g of water is 2.5 times 100 g, so 2.5 x 46 = 115 g separates. (iii) Saturated: it still holds the maximum amount of B that can dissolve at 40 degrees Celsius (241 g per 100 g of water), and the excess has come out as solid.
s: (i) 46 g per 100 g of water
(ii) 115 g in total
(iii) Saturated: it holds the maximum that dissolves at 40 degrees Celsius

questions.q: A factory makes potassium chloride crystals. It saturates 500 g of water with potassium chloride at 80 degrees Celsius and cools the solution to 20 degrees Celsius. Table 5.4 gives the solubility of potassium chloride as 54 g at 80 degrees Celsius, 40 g at 40 degrees Celsius and 35 g at 20 degrees Celsius, per 100 g of water. (a) Find the mass dissolved at 80 degrees Celsius. (b) Find the mass that stays dissolved at 20 degrees Celsius. (c) Find the mass of crystals obtained. (d) To save energy the manager suggests cooling only to 40 degrees Celsius. Find the crystals then obtained and judge whether the saving is worth losing that many crystals.
questions.a: (a) 5 x 54 = 270 g. (b) 5 x 35 = 175 g. (c) 270 - 175 = 95 g of crystals. (d) At 40 degrees Celsius, 5 x 40 = 200 g stays dissolved, so only 270 - 200 = 70 g of crystals form, 25 g fewer (about a quarter of the yield lost). Cooling to 20 degrees Celsius is better unless the energy saved costs more than 25 g of product per batch.
s: (a) 270 g dissolved at 80 degrees Celsius
(b) 175 g stays dissolved at 20 degrees Celsius
(c) 95 g of crystals
(d) Only 70 g at 40 degrees Celsius, 25 g lost; judgement given

questions.q: On the coast of Gujarat, seawater is let into shallow pans. The sun evaporates the water day after day until the remaining solution cannot dissolve any more salt. After that, crystals of common salt (sodium chloride) appear and grow and are raked up. According to Table 5.4, 100 g of water can hold at most 36.3 g of sodium chloride at 30 degrees Celsius. (a) What name is given to a solution that cannot dissolve any more salt? (b) Name the separation method in which crystals form from a saturated solution. (c) How much sodium chloride can 100 g of water hold at 30 degrees Celsius? (d) How much sodium chloride is dissolved in a pan holding 2000 g of water that is saturated at 30 degrees Celsius?
questions.a: (a) A saturated solution. (b) Crystallization (crystals form as the water evaporates from the saturated solution). (c) 36.3 g. (d) 2000 g is 20 times 100 g, so 20 x 36.3 = 726 g of sodium chloride.
s: (a) Saturated solution
(b) Crystallization

questions.q: In a distillation set-up, in which part are the vapours cooled and turned back into a liquid?
questions.a: The condenser: the vapours of the lower-boiling liquid pass through it, are cooled by circulating water or air and condense as a pure liquid.

questions.q: Using Table 5.5, chloroform boils at 61 degrees Celsius and benzene at 80 degrees Celsius. Which method should be used to separate a mixture of these two miscible liquids?
o: Fractional distillation, because their boiling points differ by less than 25 degrees Celsius
Simple distillation, because their boiling points differ by more than 15 degrees Celsius
A separating funnel, because chloroform forms a separate layer
Paper chromatography, because both liquids are colourless
questions.a: Fractional distillation, because their boiling points differ by less than 25 degrees Celsius: 80 - 61 = 19 degrees Celsius is below the about 25 degrees Celsius that simple distillation needs.

questions.q: Why do the colours in a black sketch-pen spot separate into different spots in paper chromatography?
o: The solvent carries the components up the paper at different speeds
The paper absorbs the black colour and leaves the other colours
The water reacts with the ink to make new colours
The heavier colours sink into the water and the lighter ones stay
questions.a: The solvent carries the components up the paper at different speeds: chromatography uses differences in how the components interact with the solvent and the paper, so each moves at its own rate.

questions.q: Match each term in Column I with its meaning in Column II. Column I: 1. Distillate; 2. Condenser; 3. LPG; 4. Chromatographic paper. Column II: (a) the gaseous fraction of crude petroleum filled in steel cylinders under high pressure; (b) the strip on which the components of a spot move up with the solvent; (c) the pure liquid collected after the vapour condenses; (d) the part where vapour is cooled by circulating water or air.
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b: the distillate is the condensed pure liquid, the condenser cools the vapour, LPG is the liquefied gaseous fraction of crude petroleum, and the components move up the chromatographic paper.

questions.q: True or False: 'Fractional distillation is used to separate the components of a mixture whose boiling points differ by less than 25 degrees Celsius.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Simple distillation works when the boiling points differ by at least about 25 degrees Celsius; for smaller differences, as among the fractions of crude petroleum, fractional distillation is used.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: simple distillation needs a difference of about 25 degrees Celsius; smaller differences need fractional distillation

questions.q: Two miscible liquids are mixed: liquid A boils at 64 degrees Celsius and liquid B boils at 98 degrees Celsius. (a) Can they be separated by simple distillation? Support your answer with the difference in boiling points. (b) Which liquid collects first in the receiving flask, and why?
questions.a: (a) Yes: the difference is 98 - 64 = 34 degrees Celsius, which is more than about 25 degrees Celsius. (b) Liquid A, because it has the lower boiling point, so it vaporises first and its vapour condenses in the condenser while B stays in the distillation flask.
s: (a) Yes: difference 34 degrees Celsius is above about 25 degrees Celsius
(b) A collects first, as it has the lower boiling point

questions.q: (a) Name any two products obtained from crude petroleum in a refinery. (b) Name the process used to separate crude petroleum into these products. (c) How is the gaseous fraction made into LPG?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: petroleum gas, petrol, kerosene, diesel. (b) Fractional distillation. (c) It is filled in steel cylinders under high pressure, where it gets liquefied.
s: (a) Two correct products, such as petrol and diesel
(b) Fractional distillation
(c) Filled in steel cylinders under high pressure, where it liquefies

questions.q: Two green inks are tested by paper chromatography with water. Ink P gives a single green spot that moves up the paper. Ink Q splits into a blue spot near the top and a yellow spot lower down. (i) Which ink is a mixture of dyes? Give a reason. (ii) Why do the blue and yellow spots end up at different heights? (iii) The book suggests a 2% m/v salt solution as the solvent for green food colour. How much salt is needed to make 50 mL of this solvent?
questions.a: (i) Ink Q, because it separates into two coloured components, while P shows only one. (ii) The two dyes interact differently with the solvent and the paper, so the solvent carries them up at different speeds; the blue dye moves faster. (iii) 2 g in every 100 mL, so 50 mL needs 2 x 50/100 = 1 g of salt.
s: (i) Ink Q is a mixture: it gives two spots
(ii) The dyes move at different speeds with the solvent
(iii) 1 g of salt

questions.q: Name the method you would use for each task and the one property it depends on. (a) Getting the different pigments from flower petals. (b) Getting petroleum gas, petrol, kerosene and diesel from crude petroleum. (c) Getting the water back from a copper sulfate solution. (d) Getting pure copper sulfate crystals from its hot saturated solution. (e) Separating acetone (boils at 56 degrees Celsius) from water (boils at 100 degrees Celsius).
questions.a: (a) Paper chromatography: the pigments move up the paper at different speeds. (b) Fractional distillation: the fractions have boiling points that differ by less than 25 degrees Celsius. (c) Distillation: water vaporises and is condensed, while the dissolved solid stays behind. (d) Crystallization: the solubility of copper sulfate falls as the solution cools. (e) Distillation: their boiling points differ by 44 degrees Celsius, more than about 25 degrees Celsius.
s: (a) Paper chromatography; different speeds on paper
(b) Fractional distillation; small boiling point differences
(c) Distillation; water vaporises, solid stays
(d) Crystallization; solubility falls on cooling
(e) Distillation; boiling points differ by 44 degrees Celsius

questions.q: A small paint unit in Vadodara wants to reuse its liquids instead of throwing them away. Drum 1 holds a cleaning liquid L (boils at 65 degrees Celsius) with paint solids dissolved in it. Drum 2 holds a mixture of liquid L and liquid M (boils at 118 degrees Celsius). Drum 3 holds a mixture of liquid M and liquid N (boils at 102 degrees Celsius). All the liquid pairs are miscible. The unit has a simple distillation set-up and a fractional distillation column. (a) Name the method to get liquid L back from drum 1, and say why leaving the drum open in the sun to evaporate will not do. (b) Find the difference in boiling points of the liquids in drum 2 and in drum 3. (c) Which drum can be separated by simple distillation and which needs fractional distillation? (d) In drum 2, which liquid collects first in the receiving flask, and which stays in the distillation flask?
questions.a: (a) Distillation: L vaporises, is condensed and collected, while the dissolved paint solids stay in the flask; open evaporation leaves the solids but the solvent L is lost to the air. (b) Drum 2: 118 - 65 = 53 degrees Celsius; drum 3: 118 - 102 = 16 degrees Celsius. (c) Drum 2 by simple distillation, as 53 degrees Celsius is more than about 25 degrees Celsius; drum 3 needs fractional distillation, as 16 degrees Celsius is less than 25 degrees Celsius. (d) Liquid L, which has the lower boiling point, vaporises first and collects in the receiving flask; liquid M stays in the distillation flask.
s: (a) Distillation; open evaporation loses the solvent
(b) 53 and 16 degrees Celsius
(c) Drum 2 simple, drum 3 fractional
(d) L collects first; M stays in the flask

questions.q: What is the name of the change in which a solid turns directly into vapour on heating, without passing through the liquid state?
questions.a: Sublimation: the solid changes directly to vapour on heating below its melting point, without becoming a liquid.

questions.q: Which of these mixtures can be separated using a separating funnel?
questions.a: Mustard oil and water: they are immiscible and form two separate layers, so the lower layer can be drained off through the stopcock.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A mixture of crushed camphor and sand can be separated by heating it gently in a china dish covered with an inverted funnel. Reason (R): Camphor sublimes on heating, but sand does not.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: camphor turns to vapour and deposits on the funnel, while the sand, which does not sublime, stays in the dish.

questions.q: Read the statements. I. Deposition is the change of a vapour directly into a solid on cooling. II. Camphor sublimes when it is heated below its melting point. III. In sublimation, a solid first melts into a liquid and then changes into vapour. Which of these are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Deposition is vapour turning directly into solid, and camphor sublimes on heating below its melting point. III is wrong: in sublimation the solid changes directly into vapour without passing through the liquid state.

questions.q: True or False: 'When a mixture of mustard oil and water is separated in a separating funnel, the water is collected first.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Water forms the lower layer, so when the stopcock at the bottom is opened, the water drains out first; the oil in the upper layer is collected afterwards.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: water is the lower layer, nearest the stopcock

questions.q: (a) What are immiscible liquids? (b) Give one example of a pair of immiscible liquids.
questions.a: (a) Immiscible liquids are liquids that do not mix and form separate layers. (b) Oil and water (for example, mustard oil and water).
s: (a) Liquids that do not mix and form separate layers
(b) A correct example, such as mustard oil and water

questions.q: In Activity 5.7, a mixture of crushed camphor and sand is heated gently in a china dish covered with an inverted glass funnel. (a) Where do white solid deposits appear? (b) What is left in the china dish? (c) What is the name of the change in which the camphor vapour turns back into a solid?
questions.a: (a) On the inner wall of the funnel (camphor). (b) Sand. (c) Deposition.
s: (a) On the inner wall of the funnel
(b) Sand stays in the dish
(c) Deposition

questions.q: For each mixture, name the method you would use (a separating funnel or sublimation) and the property it depends on, or say why neither works. (i) Naphthalene and sand. (ii) Mustard oil and water. (iii) Vinegar and water.
questions.a: (i) Sublimation: naphthalene sublimes on heating but sand does not. (ii) A separating funnel: the liquids are immiscible and form layers because of their different densities. (iii) Neither: vinegar and water are miscible and form one homogeneous layer, so there are no layers to drain and nothing sublimes.
s: (i) Sublimation; naphthalene sublimes, sand does not
(ii) Separating funnel; immiscible liquids of different densities
(iii) Neither: they are miscible and form one layer

questions.q: A student is given a mixture of crushed naphthalene balls and common salt. (a) Name the method she should use to separate them, and the reason it works. (b) Describe briefly how she should set up and heat the mixture. (c) Where will she collect the naphthalene, and where will the salt remain? (d) Name the two changes of state that the naphthalene goes through, in order.
questions.a: (a) Sublimation: naphthalene sublimes on heating, but common salt does not. (b) Put the mixture in a china dish on a wire gauze over a tripod stand, cover it with an inverted glass funnel whose nozzle is plugged with cotton, and heat it gently. (c) Naphthalene deposits as a solid on the inner wall of the funnel; the salt remains in the china dish. (d) Sublimation (solid to vapour) and then deposition (vapour to solid).
s: (a) Sublimation, as only naphthalene sublimes
(b) China dish, inverted funnel plugged with cotton, gentle heating
(c) Naphthalene on the funnel wall; salt in the dish
(d) Sublimation, then deposition

questions.q: In a dhaba kitchen, a 2 L can of cooking oil leaks into a bucket holding 6 L of water. The cook knows that 1 L of this oil has a mass of 920 g and 1 L of water has a mass of 1000 g. A student from the nearby school offers to recover the oil in a large vessel with a tap at the bottom, which works like the separating funnel in her laboratory. (a) What is the mass of the oil that leaked? (b) Which liquid will form the upper layer? Use the data to explain. (c) In this vessel, which liquid is drained out first, and what is done with the small portion where the two layers meet? (d) If a packet of common salt had fallen into the water instead of oil, could the salt be separated in this vessel? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 2 x 920 = 1840 g. (b) Oil: 1 L of oil (920 g) is lighter than 1 L of water (1000 g), so oil is less dense and floats as the upper layer. (c) Water, the lower layer, is drained out first; the small portion that may contain both liquids is collected separately and discarded before the oil is collected. (d) No: the salt dissolves in the water to form a homogeneous solution, a single layer, so there are no layers to drain apart.
s: (a) 1840 g of oil
(b) Oil on top: 920 g per litre is less than 1000 g per litre
(c) Water drained first; mixed middle portion discarded
(d) No: salt dissolves to form one layer (a solution)

questions.q: What is the size range of the particles in a colloid?
questions.a: 1 to 1000 nm: colloid particles are larger than those of a solution (less than 1 nm) and smaller than those of a suspension (more than 1000 nm).

questions.q: A thin beam of light is passed through four beakers. In which one will the path of the beam be visible from the side?
o: A few drops of milk stirred in water
questions.a: A few drops of milk stirred in water: milk in water is a colloid whose particles scatter light (the Tyndall effect); true solutions such as salt, sugar or copper sulfate in water do not.

questions.q: A face cream is made from 70 g of oil and 30 g of water. The water is broken up into tiny droplets that are spread all through the oil. Which description of the cream is correct?
o: Water is the dispersed phase and oil is the dispersion medium, so it is a water-in-oil emulsion like cold cream
Oil is the dispersed phase and water is the dispersion medium, so it is an oil-in-water emulsion like vanishing cream
Water is the dispersed phase and oil is the dispersion medium, so it is an oil-in-water emulsion like milk
It is a true solution, because both of its components are liquids
questions.a: Water is the dispersed phase and oil is the dispersion medium, so it is a water-in-oil emulsion like cold cream: the water droplets are the dispersed particles, the oil is the component they are spread through, and an emulsion is named by its dispersed phase in its medium.

questions.q: Match each mixture in Column I with its type in Column II. Column I: 1. Salt dissolved in water; 2. Sawdust in water; 3. Ice cream; 4. Butter. Column II: (a) water-in-oil emulsion; (b) suspension; (c) solution; (d) colloid.
questions.a: 1-c, 2-b, 3-d, 4-a: salt in water is a solution, sawdust in water is a suspension, ice cream is a colloid and butter is a water-in-oil emulsion.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Blood is not a true suspension, even though its components can be separated by centrifugation. Reason (R): The particles of a suspension are visible to the naked eye, but blood cells cannot be seen with the naked eye.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: a suspension has particles visible to the naked eye, and since blood cells are not, blood is a colloid rather than a true suspension.

questions.q: True or False: 'A beam of light passing through a true salt solution can be seen clearly from the side.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The particles of a solution are smaller than 1 nm and do not scatter light, so the path of the beam is not visible; only colloids and suspensions show the Tyndall effect.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: solution particles (less than 1 nm) do not scatter light

questions.q: (a) What is meant by the dispersed phase of a colloid? (b) What is meant by its dispersion medium?
questions.a: (a) The dispersed phase is the solute-like component, the dispersed particles in a colloid. (b) The dispersion medium is the component in which the dispersed phase is suspended.
s: (a) Dispersed phase: the solute-like dispersed particles
(b) Dispersion medium: the component in which they are suspended

questions.q: A blood sample is spun at high speed in a centrifuge. (a) Name the force that acts on the particles as the tube spins. (b) Where do the red blood cells collect, and why do they go there? (c) Very fine mud particles stay in water even after standing for hours. Explain why spinning the muddy water in a centrifuge can still separate them.
questions.a: (a) Centrifugal force, the outward force on a body moving in a circle. (b) At the bottom of the tube: they are the heavier particles, so the force moves them outwards, while the lighter plasma stays on top. (c) Spinning at high speed gives a strong outward force that pushes even fine, heavier particles to the bottom, which ordinary settling by gravity cannot do in that time.
s: (a) Centrifugal (outward) force
(b) Red blood cells at the bottom, as they are heavier
(c) The strong outward force moves fine heavier particles down that gravity alone does not

questions.q: Three kitchen mixtures are prepared: P is lemon and sugar sharbat (a true solution), Q is tea leaves stirred in water (a suspension) and R is a few drops of milk stirred in water (a colloid). (a) Arrange P, Q and R in increasing order of particle size, with the size range of each. (b) Which of them will settle if left undisturbed for some time? (c) In which of them will a beam of light have a visible path? (d) Which one will leave a residue when filtered? (e) Which one looks uniform like a solution but is not a true solution? Give the evidence that shows it.
questions.a: (a) P (less than 1 nm) < R (1 to 1000 nm) < Q (more than 1000 nm). (b) Only Q, the suspension; colloid particles in R do not settle. (c) Q and R, because colloid and suspension particles scatter light; P does not. (d) Q, since the tea leaves are large and are held back by the filter paper. (e) R: it appears uniform, but it scatters a beam of light (the Tyndall effect), which a true solution does not do.
s: (a) P < R < Q, with the size ranges
(b) Only Q settles
(c) Q and R show the beam path
(d) Q leaves a residue on filtering
(e) R, because it shows the Tyndall effect

questions.q: On a winter morning in a dusty classroom in Jaipur, a thin beam of sunlight enters through a small hole in the window shutter, and its path shows up as a bright streak. To study this, the teacher shines a laser pointer from the side through three beakers: X holds sugar dissolved in water (particles below 1 nm), Y holds a little tomato sauce stirred into water (particles about 500 nm) and Z holds chalk powder stirred into water (particles much larger than 1000 nm). (a) Name the effect seen in the classroom and the scientist who first explained it. (b) What makes the path of the sunlight visible in the classroom? (c) In which beakers will the laser path be visible? (d) After 20 minutes, which beaker will look different from the start, and what does this tell you about its type of mixture?
questions.a: (a) The Tyndall effect, first explained by John Tyndall. (b) Dust and smoke particles in the air scatter the light, making its path visible. (c) Y and Z: the colloid (about 500 nm) and the suspension (larger than 1000 nm) scatter light; the solution X does not. (d) Z: the chalk particles settle on standing, which shows that Z is a suspension; colloid particles in Y stay dispersed.
s: (a) Tyndall effect; John Tyndall
(b) Dust and smoke particles scatter the light
(c) Beakers Y and Z
(d) Z settles, so it is a suspension
